questions.q: The Industrial Disputes Act 1947 was repealed and subsumed into which legislation, effective 21 November 2025?
o: The Companies Act 2013
The Industrial Relations Code 2020
The Factories Act 1948
The Minimum Wages Act 1948
questions.src: The IR Code 2020 came into force on 21 November 2025, repealing and consolidating the ID Act 1947 along with the Trade Unions Act 1926 and the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act 1946.

questions.q: The Industrial Relations Code 2020 received Presidential Assent on:
o: 21 November 2025
28 September 2020
1 July 2024
26 January 2020
questions.src: The IR Code received Presidential Assent on 28 September 2020, though it did not come into force until 21 November 2025.

questions.q: In Bangalore Water Supply and Sewage Board v. A. Rajappa (1978), the Supreme Court held that for an undertaking to be an "industry":
o: Profit motive is absolutely essential
Profit motive is NOT necessary; systematic activity through employer-employee cooperation for producing/distributing goods or services suffices
Only manufacturing establishments qualify
The undertaking must have at least 500 employees
questions.src: This 7-judge bench ruling dramatically broadened "industry" to include hospitals, educational institutions, and similar undertakings regardless of profit motive.

questions.q: Under the ID Act, "Lay-Off," as distinguished from "Retrenchment," involves:
o: Permanent termination of employment
A TEMPORARY failure/inability to provide work, with the employment relationship CONTINUING
Voluntary resignation by the worker
Termination as a disciplinary punishment
questions.src: Lay-off is temporary — the employment relationship continues, distinguishing it from retrenchment's permanent termination.

questions.q: Under Section 25F of the ID Act, valid retrenchment of a workman with 1+ year of continuous service requires:
o: No formalities whatsoever
One month's notice (or pay in lieu), compensation of 15 days' average pay per completed year, and notice to the appropriate government
Only a verbal explanation
Approval from the workman's family
questions.src: These are the three mandatory conditions precedent under Section 25F; non-compliance renders retrenchment illegal and void.

questions.q: In State Bank of India v. N. Sundara Money (1976), the Supreme Court initially held that non-renewal of a fixed-term contract:
o: Could never amount to retrenchment under any circumstances
Amounted to "retrenchment" under Section 2(oo) as it then stood -- later partly reversed by the 1984 Amendment
Was outside the ID Act's scope entirely
Required no compensation regardless of the ruling
questions.src: This broad, worker-protective reading was later narrowed when the 1984 Amendment added Section 2(oo)(bb) excluding genuine contract non-renewal.

questions.q: Under the ID Act, government permission before lay-off/retrenchment/closure was generally required for establishments (factories/mines/plantations) employing:
o: 10 or more workers
100 or more workers
1000 or more workers
Any number of workers, without exception
questions.src: The ID Act set this threshold at 100 workers for the relevant categories of establishments.

questions.q: Under the IR Code 2020, the threshold for requiring government permission before lay-off/retrenchment/closure has been:
o: Lowered to 50 workers
RAISED to 300 workers
Abolished entirely with no threshold
Kept identical to the ID Act at 100 workers
questions.src: This is one of the most significant current-law changes -- the threshold was raised from 100 to 300 workers, giving employers below this level greater flexibility.

questions.q: Under Section 25G of the ID Act ("last come, first go"), when retrenching workmen of a particular category, the employer should ordinarily retrench:
o: The most senior workman in that category first
The workman who was LAST employed in that category, absent recorded reasons for departure
Workmen in alphabetical order
Only workmen who are trade union members
questions.src: Section 25G embodies the "last come, first go" principle, protecting workers with greater seniority absent a documented justification for deviation.

questions.q: Under the IR Code 2020, a "Re-skilling Fund" (Section 83) requires the employer to contribute, for a retrenched worker:
o: Nothing whatsoever
An amount equal to 15 days' last-drawn wages, credited to the worker within 45 days
A full year's salary immediately
Only a formal apology letter
questions.src: This is a genuinely new IR Code feature supporting retrenched workers' re-skilling/retraining through a dedicated employer-funded contribution.

questions.q: Under the ID Act, strike/lock-out notice requirements traditionally applied specifically to:
o: All industrial establishments without exception
PUBLIC UTILITY SERVICES specifically
Only government-owned enterprises
Only establishments with fewer than 10 workers
questions.src: The traditional ID Act framework limited mandatory strike notice requirements to public utility services.

questions.q: Under the IR Code 2020, strike/lock-out notice requirements have been EXPANDED to apply to:
o: No establishments at all, having been abolished
ALL industrial establishments, requiring 60 days' advance notice with the strike permissible only after 14 days
Only establishments outside major cities
Only public utility services, unchanged from the ID Act
questions.src: This is a major current-law expansion -- notice requirements under the IR Code now apply universally, not merely to public utilities.

questions.q: The IR Code's definition of "Strike" has been expanded to explicitly include:
o: Only physical work stoppage on factory premises
"Concerted casual leave" taken by 50% or more workers on a given day
Only strikes lasting more than 30 days
Only strikes called by registered political parties
questions.src: This closes a loophole -- coordinated mass casual leave is now explicitly deemed a strike under the IR Code, unlike the older ID Act framework.

questions.q: The correct sequence of the traditional dispute-settlement machinery ladder is generally:
o: Industrial Tribunal directly, with no earlier stages
Works Committee → Conciliation Officer → Board of Conciliation → Labour Court/Industrial Tribunal → National Tribunal
National Tribunal first, then working backward
There is no defined sequence at all
questions.src: This is the settled, progressively escalating dispute-resolution ladder under Indian labour law, largely retained in substance under the IR Code.

questions.q: A "National Tribunal" is constituted for disputes:
o: Involving only two employees
Of national importance, or affecting industrial establishments in more than one State
Only within a single small town
Only relating to trade union registration
questions.src: National Tribunals handle disputes with cross-state significance or genuine national importance, distinct from ordinary Labour Courts/Industrial Tribunals.

questions.q: For registration under Indian trade union law, a trade union must generally have:
o: At least 1000 members
SEVEN OR MORE members
Only management-approved members
No minimum membership requirement at all
questions.src: Seven members is the traditional minimum threshold for trade union registration, continuing under the IR Code framework.

questions.q: A registered trade union's office-bearers generally enjoy immunity from:
o: All criminal liability of any kind whatsoever
Criminal conspiracy charges for acts done in furtherance of a genuine trade dispute, unless the act itself would independently be an offence
Only civil liability, never criminal liability
No immunity of any kind
questions.src: This immunity protects legitimate trade union activity (like organising a lawful strike) from being criminalised as conspiracy, while not shielding independently unlawful acts.

questions.q: Under the IR Code, where a SINGLE registered trade union has 51% or more of workers on the muster roll, it is recognised as:
o: Only an advisory, non-binding body
The SOLE negotiating union of that establishment
Automatically dissolved
Required to merge with a rival union
questions.src: The 51% threshold grants sole recognised negotiating status -- a genuinely new, structured mechanism absent from the earlier Trade Unions Act framework.

questions.q: Where NO single trade union reaches the 51% threshold under the IR Code, the employer must instead constitute:
o: No body at all -- negotiation becomes impossible
A NEGOTIATING COUNCIL, comprising representatives from unions each holding at least 20% support
A single management-appointed representative
A court-appointed arbitrator automatically
questions.src: The negotiating council mechanism ensures structured, proportional representation even where no single union commands majority support.

questions.q: Under the ID Act/Standing Orders Act framework, formal Standing Orders were generally required for establishments with:
o: 10 or more workers
100 or more workers
1000 or more workers
No minimum threshold whatsoever
questions.src: The traditional threshold for mandatory standing orders was 100 or more workers.

questions.q: Under the IR Code 2020, the Standing Orders applicability threshold has been:
o: Lowered to 50 workers
RAISED to 300 or more workers
Left completely unchanged at 100 workers
Abolished entirely
questions.src: This mirrors the same threshold increase seen for lay-off/retrenchment/closure permission requirements -- a consistent IR Code theme of raising compliance thresholds.

questions.q: "Fixed-Term Employment," a genuinely new concept under the IR Code 2020, entitles such workers to:
o: No benefits whatsoever compared to permanent workers
The SAME statutory benefits (wages, hours, gratuity) as permanent workers, EXCEPT retrenchment compensation/notice on contract expiry
Only benefits equal to half of what permanent workers receive
Benefits only after 10 years of continuous fixed-term renewal
questions.src: Fixed-term employees receive parity with permanent workers on most benefits, but retrenchment compensation does not apply since non-renewal is excluded from the "retrenchment" definition.

questions.q: A "Grievance Redressal Committee," mandatory under the IR Code for establishments with 20+ workers, must have:
o: Only employer-appointed members with no worker representation
EQUAL representation of employer and worker sides, with proportional women's representation, up to a maximum of 10 members
Exactly 3 members regardless of establishment size
No fixed composition requirements at all
questions.src: This mandated equal-representation, gender-inclusive structure ensures a genuinely balanced internal grievance mechanism.

questions.q: Under the IR Code, the penalty structure for offences has changed such that:
o: Imprisonment now applies equally to both employers and employees for all offences
Imprisonment has been REMOVED as a penalty for employer offences, while RETAINED for illegal strike participation by employees
All penalties have been abolished entirely
Only employers, never employees, can now face any penalty
questions.src: This asymmetric change reflects the IR Code's broader "ease of doing business" orientation for employers, while maintaining deterrence against illegal strikes.

questions.q: "Industrial Dispute" under Section 2A of the ID Act extends "deemed" industrial dispute status even to disputes involving:
o: Only disputes involving an entire registered trade union
An INDIVIDUAL workman's discharge, dismissal, retrenchment, or termination, even without any other workman or union being party to it
Only disputes exceeding a specified monetary value
Only disputes between two different employers
questions.src: Section 2A provides an important protective extension, allowing individual workers to pursue statutory dispute-resolution machinery even without collective/union backing.
